synopsis: NHTSA investigations covering millions of on-road vehicles underpin the corpus's conclusion that unnecessary braking is the dominant documented automatic-braking failure mode, but Tesla's PE22-002 closed on 29 June 2026 after about 25,900 reports across 695,000 vehicles with no crashes, injuries or defect finding [f115, f1230, f11171]. Honda's investigation grew from 278 complaints in February 2022 to 1,294 across 2,997,604 vehicles in April 2024, while secondary evidence says its CMBS investigation remained open without a recall as of 2026 [f1224, f1801]. Heavy-truck evidence includes reproduced false braking on a steel trench plate and a 2021 Cascadia that avoided a stopped target at 40–85 km/h but not below 40 km/h; adaptations for stopping distance and equipment argue against directly copying passenger-car scenarios into construction or mining validation [f1812, f1329, f1233, f1527]. NHTSA documents robotic and soft-target track testing, stationary-vehicle false-positive scenarios and a −0.05 g braking-onset threshold, with track testing remaining central to its multi-year heavy-vehicle research [f562, f6192, f6193, f1331]. Its 2024 NCAP decision is an on-road consumer reference, not applicable to off-road machines, and specifies no-contact AEB tests at 40–80 km/h; FMVSS 127 cost estimates are sharply disputed at US$354.06 million annually versus an industry estimate of US$63 billion [f2838, f2629, f2886]. Regulatory certainty remains incomplete: FMVSS 127's effective date was delayed in January 2025, the final heavy-vehicle AEB rule status was not found, and the Nissan investigation status was also not found [f10866, f1333, f1806].
